knownIssues: Team comms may have provided information the demo cannot show (callouts, sound cues, teammates' kill positions).
The historical line is not assumed to be correct; it only records what this team did.
Sightings come from the demo's spotted flag, which can register enemies a player never consciously noticed.
Detected by a heuristic; not yet reviewed by a human CS2 reviewer.
Man-advantage shift: kills leave several defensible follow-ups (trade, hold, rotate); the detector does not judge which is best.
The last sighting of an enemy in T Ramp (last seen with a Desert Eagle) is 13 s old, so that position may be stale.
The follow-up sighting exists because the source team moved into position; a team that chose another line would not see it at this moment.
The follow-up information arrives less than 2 s before the next kill, leaving almost no time to react.
The follow-up is the first material change the demo shows 3-25 s later; teams may have learned of it earlier through comms.
No fact is marked inferred or unknown; the brief presents nothing as uncertain.

Follow-up depends on the team's own movement: the new information only arrived because the deciding team moved, so a player who chose a different main call might not have received it. Confirm it is fair for every main line or author a different one.

Follow-up reaction window is only 1.45 s: in the source round the situation changed again almost at once, so the responses may not be meaningfully playable. Confirm the window is long enough or author a different follow-up.

Follow-up qualities are a proposed matrix, one cell per locked main action and line now: the value of the line now after the update, minus a switching cost (10 within the same posture, 20 one step, 30 between passive and active). A reviewer should check each row: when staying with the locked line is coherent, when changing is justified, and whether the new information really supports a reversal.

Rubric ratings, evidence points and follow-up qualities are heuristic priors (see editorial.notes), not tactical judgements; time thresholds (defuse duration + 7 s, 25 s comfortable) are unreviewed assumptions.

debrief.whyItWorks: Moving weight towards where the attackers were seen puts more defenders on the likely point of contact. Here, 3 players faced 3 with about 92 seconds left.
debrief.cost: It thins another area and can be punished by a fake.
debrief.assumption: The sighting reflects the real intent and is not a fake.
debrief.breaksWhen: The attackers were showing the position to pull a rotation and hit the area that was left thin.

evidenceReview.explanation: The confirmed position of one attacker in Middle was about 2 seconds old. A sighting narrows where contact is likely, but its value falls quickly with age.
The confirmed position of one attacker in T Ramp was about 2 seconds old. A sighting narrows where contact is likely, but its value falls quickly with age.
The round clock stood near 92 seconds. The round clock bounds how long any plan can take.
It was 3 players against 3. The head count sets how many duels the team can lose and still carry out its plan.
The team had one smoke, four flashes, one HE grenade and two molotovs. The utility left sets how much of the plan can be forced rather than hoped for.

debrief.followupReview: The follow-up was judged against the line you locked. The update did not overturn the strongest line, so staying with it scored best ("Shift a player towards the latest contact"). Changing course earned the value of the new line less the time and position a switch costs, so correcting a weaker call still scored well, while abandoning a sound one or holding on to a weak one did not.
debrief.strongestAlternative: The closest alternative was to hold the current setup, keeping trades in place at the cost of the initiative.

counterfactual.changedFact: The sighting is known to be a deliberate fake.
counterfactual.effect: The rotation leaves the real target thin, and holding the setup becomes stronger.
